newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: FISCHER CONFIDENT ABOUT CHINA'S WTO MEMBERSHIP NEGOTIATIONS
Acting Prime Minister, Tim Fischer says he has been advised China will be putting more resources into negotiations on its World Trade Organisation membership.
Mr Fischer says the sooner China becomes a member of the WTO, the better.
He says Hong Kong's membership will continue under Chinese sovereignty, and he expects negotiations on China's membership to make significant progress this year.
Mr Fischer says he is confident there will be an improved offer from China in the near future.
MINISTER CONCERNED ABOUT MILLENNIUM BUG
Federal Science minister, Peter McGauran, says he's not convinced business will be prepared in time to cope with the Millenium Bug.
Mr McGauran says many computer systems need to be rewritten or replaced to cope with date entries for the year 2000 and beyond.
He says if the problem's not fixed, on January the first, 2000 payments will cease, data systems will crash or revert back 100 years and major projects will grind to a halt.
Mr McGauran says while large organisations are taking the issue seriously, anecdotal evidence suggests many smaller ones don't fully appreciate the problem.
He's warned businesses that haven't taken the necessary steps could face financial ruin, because of legal action taken against them, and a flow-on effect to other businesses and services.
DISAPPEARANCE OF MOE TODDLER NOW A MURDER INVESTIGATION
Victorian police say the disappearance of Moe toddler, Jaidyn Leskie is probably one of the most complex they have ever had to investigate.
Police are now treating the disappearance as murder.
The 14 month old boy disappeared from a house in the Latrobe Valley town where he was being cared for by his mother's boyfriend 17 days ago.
Police acting commander Peter Blick has travelled to Moe to offer encouragement and thanks to officers on the case.
Mr Blick says the investigation has been very trying, but police will invest more effort and resources until they achieve a conviction.
He says the case is full of complexities, and has been hampered by a lot of misinformation.
BANK EXECUTIVE COMMITTED FOR TRIAL ON INSIDER TRADING CHARGES
A Macquarie Bank executive has been committed to stand trial in the New South Wales District Court, on a charge of insider trading.
A Sydney magistrate has found that the evidence against 36 year old Simon Hannes is capable of satisfying a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions alleges Mr Hannes traded in TNT stock late last year while his employer was an advisor on a foreign takeover bid for the transport group.
The maximum penalty for insider trading is five years imprisonment, and/or a 200-thousand-dollar fine.
FULL ADVERTISING TO BE ALLOWED ON SBS RADIO PROGRAMMES
SBS has decided to allow full advertising on its radio programs.
Until now advertising has been restricted to paid information campaigns by government departments, agencies and non-profit organisations; and soccer broadcasts.
As a result of the policy change up to five minutes of advertising per hour will be heard on SBS Radio programs.
The decision to allow full advertising comes in the context of budget cut-backs and, and the need to replace ageing equipment.
WOOLDRIDGE LAUNCHES RECRUITMENT CAMPAIGN FOR PRIVATE HEALTH COVER
The Federal Health Minister has launched a $3 million advertising campaign promoting private health cover.
The campaign promotes private health insurance on the basis it will give people faster access to elective surgery.
Michael Wooldridge says the Public Hospital System can't cope with the two percent annual drop out rate from the private health insurance system.
Dr Wooldridge that needs to stop, and he's certain his efforts will lead to that.
The Minister says there is a lot of interest from people wanting to rejoin health funds.
He rejects suggestions by the Doctors' Reform Society that wealthy people would have better access than poor people, saying that will only happen when people don't have choice.
ADAMS VISA BEING RECONSIDERED BY FEDERAL COURT
The Federal Court will reveal tomorrow whether Sinn Fein leader, Gerry Adams, will be allowed to enter Australia.
The Court is considering an appeal after Mr Adams' application, for a temporary business visa, was rejected last year by Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock.
Mr Adams had intended to visit Australia last year to promote a book.
The court heard the application was rejected on the grounds that Mr Adams was not of good character because of his association with the provisional IRA.

Mr Adams' lawyers have applied to the court to order the release of information used by Mr Ruddock to make his decision. They told the court the Minister did not have enough factual evidence to tie Mr Adams to the IRA, and questioned whether an association with the IRA is enough to determine Mr Adams' character.
Justice Drummond has reserved his decision until tomorrow. - - - -
EMPLOYMENT MINISTER SAYS CES REFORMS COULD START THIS YEAR
The Federal Employment Minister says the new competitive employment market resulting from the reforms of the CES, could start being implemented as early as December this year.
The reforms were set to begin in March next year, but Amanda Vanstone says because of the Senate's attempts to frustrate the process, the Government may have to circumvent the Senate.
Senator Vanstone says the reforms can be achieved much earlier by using existing legislation, rather than getting the reform bill up.
She says the Government will use the same legislation the former Labor government used to deliver its Working Nation programme.
The Minister says while there may need to be some minor changes, there will be no change in direction.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
